Gibson Nzimande

By: Jabulile Mbatha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From wastepicker to Master's degree graduate, Gibson Nzimande is a steadfast student who excelled despite adversities.

Unique Selling Point:
Only 6% of South Africans have university degrees, and in numbers that is 1,7 million people in a country of 59,39 million. This is according to the Higher Education Department in 2021. One of those people is Gibson Nzimande, with all odds stacked against him, he made it through and is on his way to a PhD.

Summary:
This is the story of Gibson Nzimande who grew up in a blended family, living a normal life of a middle-class family in a house in Katlehong, the East of Johannesburg.

One day his normal life was turned upside down. This was four years ago. He not only lost his mother but was thrown to the streets, abandoned by his six siblings and father.

He was forced into street life, during the day collecting recyclables from the streets of Sandton and getting paid for it in Alex where there are several recycling centers. At night he slept under a tree on Rivonia Road.

He decided the only thing that would save him from the street life was education so he went to a local library and enrolled at the University of Johannesburg to study. Today he holds a Masters's degree in History, with plans to pursue his PhD.

He cleaned up with the help of petrol attendants who would sneak in to get hot water for him to bathe, he would buy food and study materials with the money from recycling and study at a bench near the garage.

He says during the day he would collect waste and at night he studied with the help of the petrol station's lights.

His former lecturer took him out of the streets after hearing his story and helped him scrap his debt with the university while getting more funding for him to study further and get accommodation.

He fought hard to stay away from crime and drugs that he was constantly exposed to, in street life. That was not the only challenge he was faced with but the severe poverty, but through it all he preserved and became the success he is today.

- I would tell the story through a recreation of images by following the day in the life of a waste picker. We met with one of his old friends who has agreed to this. This includes close-up shots of the sack they use to carry the recyclables, him getting up to go collect, long shots of him passing through places like Sandton City pulling his trolley and later delivering them to be weighed so he can get paid.
This is against the backdrop of his interview about his old life.

- An interview with a petrol attendant (Johannes) who also helped him with food and water near where he used to sleep. I would like to film the petrol station at night to show what lighting Gibson had to work with. Perhaps a timelapse would be a creative way to demonstrate this.

- A childhood friend (Tumelo Ntoyi) who can refer us to the background story of Gibson, how they grew up, and his account of how the transition affected Gibson. This is the closest person to being family as his whole family abandoned him and did not even reconcile with him post-graduation as one would expect. I would like to film them revisiting where they used to live, where they would go by bread for example, generic shots of a playground or park they used to visit. Just to reminisce of their old lives in the township growing up.

- The lecturer Prof Thembisa at the university, general cutaways of the lecture hall and them wokring and of the university.

- Additional shots are of the city life, the hustle and bustle, moving taxis, and street vendors.

- General shots of the groups of the waste-pickers sitting down and eating or moving together with their trolleys in groups, also shots of them at the scrap yards.

- The new life of Gibson in his small room at the student res, and shots of him going to the library living his new life. He stays in a residence in the city.

- Additional pictures of him in his old life.

- Graduation pictures.


Further information:
Visuals that will incorporate the presenter:

Opening shot: drone footage of Johannesburg CBD - an ariel view that slowly zooms in and we get into the street where we see a homeless guy waking up and the symbol of it being time to wake up is the nat sound of birds and taxis hooting and people shouting and even others pulling their trolleys

*Note that the homeless guy we used is for re-enactments

We have him fold his blankets and he hides them in hopes of getting them in the same place because it’s always a battle for space

No kitchen, no bed, no walls, or privacy, no bathroom, no food, no water. What would you do if your morning started here? VO This
We zoom out and have him continue in the background

Presenter on scene under the bridge where this guy in the back ground has woken up from...
*On some level we all are familiar with the concept of fighting for survival but not like this… where Gibson Nzimande spent his last five years but it wasn’t always like this* Link

To change scenes we can use a passing taxi as a transition one from town to Katlehong- when we chop into the scene of Katlehong after the taxi passes and we see Gibson, he walks towards his old home and looking very sad and looking like he is in deep thought, close up shots and presenters walks to meet him and they both look at the house and he says that’s how his problems started

Then it’s a walking interview and we show more of the township

Talk about growing up here and challenges he faced

They walked towards the shops where we now meet Tumelo and we talk about their friendship and what he observed seeing Gibson grow up here. Also about their undergrad years. It would be nice seeing them interact as friends, show places where they used to go to growing up eg, soccer field

Tumelo must leave us with a cliffhanger - something like "and then it happened and we lost touch with Gibson for years*

Hand shots, close ups

Back to presenter and Gibson he then explains how he got kicked out.

We use their feet to transition to Joburg as a symbol of his long walk to this new life

He was kicked out and he literally walked to Joburg

*Pushed unexpectedly into the busy streets of Joburg, uncertain of where to turn and what to do* Thought about link- presenter back on scene in town

Link about homelessness in SA-
*The question can be how often do we see people in the street and wonder what their story is? Get the stats on how many people have disputes about homes and many of them end up in the streets because of it. Then the expert says a byte on this.

Get Nat sounds of hawkers and police and hooting of cars and show these visuals in a nice fast way- to demonstrate that it was overwhelming and all quick for him

This can also be a visual of him standing and watching the busy Joburg Streets- timelapse maybe

Get Gibson to now talk (voice in background) about his journey and the struggle of street life but also how his day in a life as a student and a wastepicker this is through the visuals of the re-enactment then we meet the presenter at the recycling hubs she can give us some info on how much people make from recycling and match it to what you can afford to buy in a day for food with that money* Link

Mention that the person who is doing the re-enactment is a friend of Gibson who wasn’t able to get out of this situation like he did.

Then we move into a late afternoon scene, I would like a link of the presenter by the petrol station with the darkness of the night to show that Gibson had to do all that he could to get some lighting, then we have interview of presenter with the petrol attendant who used to help Gibson out.

Then we VO the progression of his success to graduation with the archive footage then...

The last part of it will be with the supervisor at the university, the presenter does a short link to intro the supervisor, we can interchange this interview with the visuals of his new life and close with a closing link

Script:


Gibson Nzimande script

VO 1: Being homeless in Johannesburg can be gruelling… but one man's life is showing that it doesn’t have to be the end.

Nat sound & visuals of the guy waking up, people pushing trolleys, city life

VO 2: When a young man called Gibson Nzimande lost his home, and was forced to live here, he was confronted with every temptation the streets can offer: crime … drugs … anything for a temporary fix.

But by persisting in a way few are prepared to, Gibson transformed his life, one difficult day at a time.

PRESENTER Link 1253 :@ 0:3 Imagine living, sleeping, and waking up in the dirt and stench that is the Johannesburg CBD and still trying to make something out of your life, well one man had an unwavering determination, not just to survive the streets but also to achieve something that some would consider unattainable for someone in his situation.

VO 4: Gibson comes from sprawling Katlehong in the East Rand.

GIBSON: I grew up in a poverty-stricken home and the only thing my grandmother used to tell me is that school is important, it's the only tool to escape from poverty.

VO 5: Home was never a happy place. He was studying at the University of Johannesburg… when without warning, his mother passed away, ripping apart his already tenuous existence.

GIBSON: I was fascinated by historical events so I wanted to further my studies in history. My plan was to study political science or history
CLAIRE: How would you say the passing of your mother changed the direction of your life?
GIBSON: That’s when I saw life, I have to pull up my socks, I have to study hard so that
I can make sure everything is fine in my life…I hustled R1500 for registration. That’s when I managed to get a bursary from Ekhuruleni

VO 6: His bursary was just enough to kickstart a BA degree - but not nearly enough to afford rent. His best friend then and now: Tumelo Ntoyi.
TUMELO: Gibson and I are very close he knows my number off by heart
VO 7: Although they studied together for years - Gibson was too embarrassed to tell Tumelo his biggest secret.


GIBSON: Beginning of 2020 thats when I was officially in the streets
TUMELO: I never knew Gibson is homeless up until I got a call from one of the guys I know in the township who said “your best friend is homeless” and I wondered how
CLAIRE: how did that make you feel that he is living in the streets?
TUMELO: I was so touched I cried that day not understanding what kind of person Gibson is because we’ve been through good and bad times and now that he was facing such difficulties why didn’t he tell me?

VO 8: Not willing to let it destroy him, Gibson made a trolley - from scrap - and
joined thousands of waste-pickers who collect and sell recyclables at the citys rubbish dumps.

GIBSON: A trolley, a bucket, two trousers and the bucket I used had soap, a wash cloth and toiletries, my degrees, and my diary because each and every year from high school level I used to have a diary. Because each and every year - fron high school level - I used to have a diary to jot down my stuff.

VO 9: Wastepicker by day. Student by night. Always on edge.

GIBSON: remember if you are living on the street you are kind of like a nomad, there’s no proper place for you, you sleep everywhere like whenever you can catch some sleep, that’s your home… police can come anytime and evict you.

VO 10: His luck only began turning when he carved out a home of sorts under a tree opposite a petrol station in Sandton. Johannes Lekganyane was the supervisor.

JOHANNES: One thing that really attracted me to him. It was his humbleness. Every time when he was sitting on the corner, he will be reading something
CLAIRE: You as Johannes, you could have very easily have said..go away, leave this place - people do that.
JOHANNES: I will say maybe it was God doing things his way maybe it was God that Gibson ended up here. The culture here is beautiful. You know, the culture here is about people, we were in the business of helping people. And I will say, we are I mean, the staff. I mean, we learned this from our bosses, they look after everyone.

VO 12: All the while, Gibson’s debt at UJ was escalating - but his history professor, Thembisa Waetjen took him under her wing.

PROF: I think Gibson’s life experience, the challenges he faced, he has translated that into an advantage, an academic advantage in two ways. The first way is that its giving him some empathy for his research subjects, his passion about wanting to humanize the story of people who are often morally condemned or marginalized and maybe who face hardships like himself. The second way I think i that the instinct to survive has translated to a determination to succeed

VO: GIbson seldom earned more than R50 a day.

CLAIRE LINK: Do you know what I have realized is that you and I are very guilty of making sweeping judgments of wastepickers and people experiencing homelessness, but just because we see them living in such a tough situation, it doesn't mean that they have lost hope for their own lives.

GIBSON: I had a plan, a daily plan, sometimes, especially on Wednesdays and Thursdays I’d go to the library and research and then Friday with the money I am earning from the scrap I’d go to internet cafe and apply for jobs, and search for things.

VO 15: Gibson seldom earned even R50 a day… finally, it all paid off when UJ scrapped his staggering debt two years ago, and undertook to fund his Masters Degree. For the first time, he could even afford a room again.

JOHANNES: Don’t believe Gibson made it..17:00 Yeah, definitely. I mean, even now, I can still believe it. I don't believe Gibson made it. That’s what i learned from the Gibson Nzimande thing.. 13:25 So if you really believe in your dreams, go for it. And thats what I learned about the whole Gibson Nzimande thing. What a beautiful story.
PROF: There were moments where he felt like he might just drop out and he was actually feeling like it would be better to get back to the streets
CLAIRE: Really?
PROF: I think that it’s hard to understand when you haven't lived that life, that losing that life for whatever reason, even if you say it was not valuable it is a certain kind of independence.
TUMELO: Gibson is a very resilient individual - we call him ‘inja yeainganga’ [wild dog] which simply means someone who fights hard and stay resilient..

BIG MOMENT MUSIC
Upsound his graduation for his masters degree: Musawenkosi Gibson Nzimande… claps hands

GIBSON: For me I just told myself, I know I'm in this situation but if only I can just do my masters it will be easier for me to do my PhD and become a historian as I wanted to be a social scientist " Thats when I registered for my masters.
CLAIRE: Are you aware people dont think the same?
GIBSON: material things are nothing from my side but knowledge is power. I would rather die poor than without knowledge


Closing 16: At last Gibson is able stop to juggling such vastly different worlds… Joburg’s rough streets and his precious books.. one step closer to becoming Doctor Nzimande.

What a beautiful story. PROF: There were moments where he felt like he might just drop out and he was actually feeling like it would be better to get back to the streets CLAIRE: Really? PROF: I think that it’s hard to understand when you haven't lived that life, that losing that life for whatever reason, even if you say it was not valuable it is a certain kind of independence. TUMELO: Gibson is a very resilient individual - we call him ‘inja yeainganga’ [wild dog] which simply means someone who fights hard and stay resilient.. BIG MOMENT MUSIC Upsound his graduation for his masters degree: Musawenkosi Gibson Nzimande… claps hands GIBSON: For me I just told myself, I know I'm in this situation but if only I can just do my masters it will be easier for me to do my PhD and become a historian as I wanted to be a social scientist " Thats when I registered for my masters. CLAIRE: Are you aware people dont think the same? GIBSON: material things are nothing from my side but knowledge is power. I would rather die poor than without knowledge Closing 16: At last Gibson is able stop to juggling such vastly different worlds… Joburg’s rough streets and his precious books.. one step closer to becoming Doctor Nzimande.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From wastepicker to Master's degree graduate, Gibson Nzimande is a steadfast student who excelled despite adversities.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Only 6% of South Africans have university degrees, and in numbers that is 1,7 million people in a country of 59,39 million. This is according to the Higher Education Department in 2021. One of those people is Gibson Nzimande, with all odds stacked against him, he made it through and is on his way to a PhD.
metadata.Summary: This is the story of Gibson Nzimande who grew up in a blended family, living a normal life of a middle-class family in a house in Katlehong, the East of Johannesburg. One day his normal life was turned upside down. This was four years ago. He not only lost his mother but was thrown to the streets, abandoned by his six siblings and father. He was forced into street life, during the day collecting recyclables from the streets of Sandton and getting paid for it in Alex where there are several recycling centers. At night he slept under a tree on Rivonia Road. He decided the only thing that would save him from the street life was education so he went to a local library and enrolled at the University of Johannesburg to study. Today he holds a Masters's degree in History, with plans to pursue his PhD. He cleaned up with the help of petrol attendants who would sneak in to get hot water for him to bathe, he would buy food and study materials with the money from recycling and study at a bench near the garage. He says during the day he would collect waste and at night he studied with the help of the petrol station's lights. His former lecturer took him out of the streets after hearing his story and helped him scrap his debt with the university while getting more funding for him to study further and get accommodation. He fought hard to stay away from crime and drugs that he was constantly exposed to, in street life. That was not the only challenge he was faced with but the severe poverty, but through it all he preserved and became the success he is today. - I would tell the story through a recreation of images by following the day in the life of a waste picker. We met with one of his old friends who has agreed to this. This includes close-up shots of the sack they use to carry the recyclables, him getting up to go collect, long shots of him passing through places like Sandton City pulling his trolley and later delivering them to be weighed so he can get paid. This is against the backdrop of his interview about his old life. - An interview with a petrol attendant (Johannes) who also helped him with food and water near where he used to sleep. I would like to film the petrol station at night to show what lighting Gibson had to work with. Perhaps a timelapse would be a creative way to demonstrate this. - A childhood friend (Tumelo Ntoyi) who can refer us to the background story of Gibson, how they grew up, and his account of how the transition affected Gibson. This is the closest person to being family as his whole family abandoned him and did not even reconcile with him post-graduation as one would expect. I would like to film them revisiting where they used to live, where they would go by bread for example, generic shots of a playground or park they used to visit. Just to reminisce of their old lives in the township growing up. - The lecturer Prof Thembisa at the university, general cutaways of the lecture hall and them wokring and of the university. - Additional shots are of the city life, the hustle and bustle, moving taxis, and street vendors. - General shots of the groups of the waste-pickers sitting down and eating or moving together with their trolleys in groups, also shots of them at the scrap yards. - The new life of Gibson in his small room at the student res, and shots of him going to the library living his new life. He stays in a residence in the city. - Additional pictures of him in his old life. - Graduation pictures.
